newsitem.title: USA: Stock market crash would not hurt economy - UCLA.
newsitem.headline: Stock market crash would not hurt economy - UCLA.

text.p: The U.S. economy would not be hurt by a sharp decline in the stock market, according to a study to be released Wednesday by economists at the University of California Los Angeles.

In fact, the economists said a decline of more than 30 percent in the Dow Jones Industrial Average would probably stimulate the economy by pushing interest rates lower, extending the rally in the bond market and providing pension fund managers with the opportunity to acquire equities with better yields.
"A decent collapse in the stock market would be nice right now," the economists said in their study. "We need a break for a change."

The study said a 36 percent drop in the stock market, similar to the decline that happened between August 25 and October 19, 1987, would take the Dow Jones Industrial Average to 4160 from around 6500, almost 2.5 times the bottom reached in the October 1987 crash.
The quarterly econimic study said the U.S. economy should grow around 2.5 percent next year, with no apparent threat of inflation.

The study said real gross domestic product should continue to grow moderately next year and inflation should remain low, with consumer prices rising 2.8 percent in 1997. Producer prices are expected to rise only one percent in 1997.
The economists said the moderate rate of inflation is not expected to put pressure on the Federal Reserve Bank to be aggressive when it comes to interest rates.

On Tuesday, the Federal Reserve opted to hold interest rates steady, leaving the key federal funds rate that commerical banks charge each other for overnight loans at 5.25 percent and the discount rate that the Fed charges banks for money at 5.0 percent.

The UCLA study said corporate pre-tax profits are expected to perk up to a six percent growth rate next year, compared with a modest three percent increase in 1996. However, that is still down from the 13 percent growth experienced in 1995.
The growth rate for business fixed investment will remain at around 6.3 percent in 1997, about the same as in 1996, but down from 9.5 percent in 1995.
Housing starts will average around 1.48 million units in 1997, almost the same as this year's starts of 1.47 million. The effective mortgage rate is expected to fall to 7.22 percent in 1997.

Real consumer spending for goods and services is expected to grow at 2.4 percent next year, slightly below the real GDP growth. Unemployment is expected to fall next year to 5.2 percent and then rise to 5.3 percent in 1998.
